If it weren’t so dystopian, it might have been called calm. The road leading to the protest site at Jantar Mantar had been barricaded at both ends. New surveillance cameras and loudspeakers were strapped to trees every few hundred metres. From the speakers, a woman’s voice, unhurried and polite, warned people not to join the next day’s demonstration. Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita was in force, she said. Gatherings of five or more, slogans, and protest symbols were prohibited. Then the message played again, and again, in a continuous loop. Closer to Jantar Mantar, a policeman stood over a labourer as he welded four rows of metal barricades into one, so that no protester could drag them apart. On October 9, new surveillance cameras and loudspeakers were strapped to trees and electric posts every few hundred metres. Metal barricades were welded together so that protesters could not drag them apart. Jantar Mantar is not where the Prime Minister lives. It is not where Gyanesh Kumar lives or where the Election Commission sits. It is simply the place the government itself set aside for dissent. Over time, this site has become where India brings what it cannot take anywhere else. For anyone with a prayer, a petition, or a protest, all roads usually lead to Jantar Mantar. But, on the eve of this protest — no roads led to Jantar Mantar. Instead, the entire city was swarming with thousands of security personnel. Hundreds of trains were cancelled. The borders of the capital were sealed. More than 50 metro stations were shut, and the traffic that remained was watched closely. The internet was going to be suspended in central Delhi the next day. The Delhi police made it clear that they had not granted permission for the protest. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) responded by saying they only informed the police. “We’ve been brainwashed all these years to think that to protest against the government, we need their permission first. items.title: BREAKING: Prima facie contempt case made out over Delhi Metro restrictions during protests, says Supreme Court
items.summary: The Supreme Court has held that a prima facie case of contempt of court has been made out over the alleged violation of its October 9 directions concerning restrictions on Metro and railway services in Delhi during the October 10 protests. A Bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana recorded the finding in its written order following a special Sunday hearing on a contempt petition filed by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi. The contempt plea was filed against Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) Chairperson D Thara. Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Justice V Mohana " Having considered the submissions of the learned counsel for the parties and perused the averments in the Contempt Petition, we are of the opinion that the petitioners have made out a prima facie case. Accordingly, we issue notice upon the alleged contemnors ," the Court said. The alleged contemnors have been directed to file counter-affidavits, along with a report on compliance with the Court's October 9 order, by October 13. Their personal appearance has been dispensed with for the time being. The contempt petition alleged that authorities went ahead with restrictions on public transport despite the Supreme Court's earlier directions against a complete prohibition on Metro and railway operations during protests seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. The protests come amid growing criticism of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls undertaken by the Election Commission of India. On October 9, the Supreme Court had observed that notifications restricting public transport ahead of October 10 protests appeared to be overreaching. It had directed the authorities to reconsider the proposed closure of 57 Metro stations, permit regulated train operations and widely publicise revised decisions to minimise inconvenience to commuters. A contempt of court petition was filed on October 10, alleging that Delhi Metro stations remained closed despite the Court's October 9 order against a complete shutdown of public transport. During Sunday's hearing of the matter, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta disputed the allegations of non-compliance with the October 9 directions. He submitted that Delhi Metro services had operated normally, although 45 of 303 stations had been closed to maintain law and order. items.title: Delhi protests: Supreme Court orders no detentions, traffic or metro restrictions except as per law
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Sunday asked Delhi authorities to explain why contempt of court action should not be initiated against them for closure of metro stations on October 10 amid the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests. A total of 45 metro stations, mostly in and around Central Delhi, were shut on October 10 in view of the protests at Jantar Mantar against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The closure of metro stations along with detention of key CJP leaders and opposition members had led to a flurry of petitions before the Supreme Court. The principal matter before the Court was a contempt petition filed by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi against Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation Chairperson D Thara. The plea alleged that Delhi Metro stations remained closed on Sunday despite the Supreme Court's October 9 saying there shouldn't be complete shutdown of public transport ahead of the protests. At a special sitting held on Sunday, a Bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana sought responses from the government authorities on the closure of metro stations. "We direct the authorities concerned to submit a short affidavit showing cause why contempt proceedings shall not be initiated. Issue notice upon the alleged contemnors to file an affidavit in response to the contempt petition and also submit a compliance report in respect of the terms of the order as aforesaid," the Court directed. An out-of-breath and visibly distressed Brittas told the media , "I was shoved onto a seat and pinned down by four CRPF personnel. He then told them to let me go right away, or each of them would be suspended. That is when they let me off here." The DCP saw the assault through the camera attached to one of the men, Brittas clarified. "They beat him also," Brittas said, pointing to a man sitting next to him. “It was only this man who was there to help me, I do not even know his name,” Brittas said, before turning to the man and asking for his name. "Sajid Hussein," he replied. "It was because of him that I was able to get off. He took the phone when the DCP called," Brittas added. "I repeatedly told them that I am an MP and showed them my ID card. This is my situation despite being an MP. I am not able to talk more," Brittas said, seated on the pavement, breathing heavily. All three worked at a shop in Thrikkakara and were returning towards Athani after stopping for tea near the Cochin International Airport. items.title: Karnataka HC stays FIRs against BJP booth agents over Form 7 objections in Malleswaram
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court has stayed two FIRs registered against BJP Booth Level Agents accused of trying to delete voters' names from electoral rolls by filing bulk Form 7 objections during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in the Malleswaram Assembly Constituency. Justice Anant Ramanath Hegde granted the interim relief on two separate writ petitions filed by the agents on Saturday, October 10, LiveLaw reported . Form 7 is used to object to the inclusion of a name in the rolls or to seek deletion of an entry. The petitioners, GS Vasanthalakshmi and Deepak Singh R, sought the quashing of the FIRs registered at the Vyalikaval and Yeshwanthpura police stations in Bengaluru. Vasanthalakshmi is accused of filing Form 7 objections for 778 voters across eight booths and Deepak Singh R of attempting to remove 136 voters in Booth 68 by describing the electors as "absent" or "permanently shifted", even though they allegedly continued to reside in the constituency. The FIRs alleged that the signatures on several of the forms differed from one another. This, the complaint said, pointed to the possibility that either the petitioners or someone else had forged the signatures with the intent of furnishing false information through the applications. Before the High Court, the petitioners argued that the offences alleged in connection with Form 7 are non-cognizable and bailable. They contended that such offences cannot be investigated by the police without an order from a Magistrate under Section 174(2) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023. Accepting the plea for interim protection, the court stayed the operation of both FIRs. Allegations of attempts to delete the names of voters en masse through Form 7 have emerged across the state in several Assembly constituencies, such as Ballari, Malleswaram, Koppa, Basavakalyan, Babaleshwar, Bhalki, Shivamogga, and Belthangady. In several instances, the Karnataka police have filed FIRs, invoking provisions of cheating and fraud in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). items.title: Eerie calm to the violence of lathis: Walking through Delhi on October 9 and 10
items.summary: On October 9, as the sun gently set over central Delhi, the city fell into an unusually quiet lull. It was the day before the protests demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and a rollback of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. If it weren’t so dystopian, it might have been called calm. The road leading to the protest site at Jantar Mantar had been barricaded at both ends. New surveillance cameras and loudspeakers were strapped to trees every few hundred metres. From the speakers, a woman’s voice, unhurried and polite, warned people not to join the next day’s demonstration. Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita was in force, she said. Gatherings of five or more, slogans, and protest symbols were prohibited. Then the message played again, and again, in a continuous loop. Closer to Jantar Mantar, a policeman stood over a labourer as he welded four rows of metal barricades into one, so that no protester could drag them apart. On October 9, new surveillance cameras and loudspeakers were strapped to trees and electric posts every few hundred metres Metal barricades were welded together so that protesters could not drag them apart Jantar Mantar is not where the Prime Minister lives. It is not where Gyanesh Kumar lives or where the Election Commission sits. It is simply the place the government itself set aside for dissent. Over time, this site has become where India brings what it cannot take anywhere else. For anyone with a prayer, a petition, or a protest, all roads usually lead to Jantar Mantar. But, on the eve of this protest — no roads led to Jantar Mantar. Instead, the entire city was swarming with thousands of security personnel. Hundreds of trains were cancelled. The borders of the capital were sealed. More than 50 metro stations were shut, and the traffic that remained was watched closely. The internet was going to be suspended in central Delhi the next day.
